candidates.title: Inside Photo Metadata
candidates.plainSentence: A lesson that lets you open a sample photo, see its hidden location and camera data, and remove it without touching the picture.
candidates.pitch: Open a built-in sample photo and see its file laid out as a strip of labelled byte segments, then click the Exif segment to read the hidden location, camera, date and software fields in plain words. Delete segments with a switch and watch a SHA-256 fingerprint of the compressed picture data stay identical while the file shrinks, with the hash routine checked live against NIST example values. Then meet the traps: a stale thumbnail that still shows the uncropped scene, a rotation tag whose removal turns a photo sideways, and what no stripping can hide.
candidates.firstMinute: The page opens with a sample photo already parsed: a coloured strip of file segments, a card reading 'taken at these coordinates with this camera on this date', and a Remove hidden data switch. Flipping the switch shows the card empty, the file size drop, and two matching SHA-256 fingerprints labelled 'picture data before' and 'after'. No reading is needed for that first success.
conceptsToLearn: A photo file holds the picture and, separately, a block of notes about it
candidates.whyNow: Timeless. Photos are shared every day, and almost nobody has seen what is inside the file; the lesson shows it with a real parser instead of a diagram.

purposeDetail.concept: A JPEG file is a sequence of marker-delimited segments. The compressed picture data (the scan after the start-of-scan header, up to the end marker) is separate from the metadata segments, such as the Exif block in APP1 which holds a small TIFF-style directory of fields (camera, time, GPS sub-directory, thumbnail). Deleting metadata segments leaves the compressed picture bytes untouched, so it is lossless, and a hash of those bytes proves it.
purposeDetail.whyNiche: Most explanations either say 'photos contain EXIF, remove it' with no look inside, or dive into the raw specification. Free web tools hide the mechanism, and many re-save the picture, so people cannot tell whether quality was lost or what was actually removed.
purposeDetail.audience: Curious non-experts who share photos online, plus students and developers who have never opened a JPEG file's bytes.
prerequisites: Know that a photo can be saved as a .jpg file
Know what a hash is only loosely: a short fingerprint of some bytes (the page defines it)
misconceptions: Cropping or blurring a photo also removes what was cut, because the file only holds the visible picture (an embedded thumbnail can still show the original)
Removing metadata is always harmless (dropping the orientation tag without rotating the pixels can make the photo display sideways)
Removing metadata means re-saving the picture, which must lower its quality (segment deletion leaves the compressed picture data byte-identical)
purposeDetail.ahaMoment: The picture data hash is identical before and after, yet the location, camera and a hidden thumbnail are gone: the secrets and the picture were never the same bytes.
demos: 1. Byte strip: the sample file drawn as proportional coloured segments (start marker, JFIF header, Exif block, quantisation and Huffman tables, frame header, scan, end marker); click one to see its first bytes in hex and a plain-English label

2. Field reader: the Exif block decoded into a readable list (GPS, camera, date, software), with a worked example turning degrees-minutes-seconds and the N/S/E/W reference letters into decimal coordinates, and a pointer-following animation from the header to the GPS directory
3. Thumbnail trap: the sample photo is cropped but its embedded thumbnail still shows the uncropped scene; deleting the thumbnail makes it disappear

4. Strip and prove: switches per segment group (GPS only, camera and time, thumbnail, all Exif, comments), live byte count, SHA-256 of the whole file (changes) versus SHA-256 of the scan bytes (does not), plus a self-check panel that runs the SHA-256 routine on the NIST example messages
5. The rotation catch: a sample stored sideways with an orientation tag; removing the tag makes it appear turned, with the safe options explained
6. What stays: a picture whose street sign, shadow and window reflection give the place away without any metadata, so the visitor sees stripping is not anonymity
7. Try your own (behind a More toggle): drop JPEG files to read their fields and download cleaned copies made by deleting segments only; nothing leaves the browser
checkQuestions: You delete the GPS fields from a photo. Does the hash of the compressed picture data change, and why?
A friend crops a face out of a photo and posts the original file. What inside the file might still show the face?
Why can removing a rotation tag make a photo look sideways even though no pixel changed?
A cleaned photo still shows your house number on the door. Which part of the page's lesson does that illustrate?

research.summary: The file layout is documented consistently: a JPEG is a chain of marker segments from the start marker to the end marker, with the compressed scan after the scan header, and Exif lives in an APP1 segment that holds a TIFF-style directory with a GPS sub-directory and a thumbnail directory. NIST publishes the SHA-256 example value for the three-letter message 'abc', and an independent test-vector page agrees, so the hash can be checked against a named oracle. Stale embedded thumbnails after cropping are documented by a security advisory and a Microsoft engineer's blog, and removing the orientation tag without rotating pixels is a documented cause of sideways images. Lossless metadata removal is what the jpegtran manual describes for metadata. Free web tools exist, so the page is a lesson that shows its working, not a competitor tool.

sources.title: The Metadata in JPEG files (Exiv2 wiki)
sources.snippet: Describes the JPEG segment layout: start marker, header segments, baseline frame header, single scan, and where Exif sits; notes Exif is meant to come first but many files put a JFIF header first.
sources.note: Segment structure and the Exif-after-JFIF ordering caveat

sources.title: Exif (Wikipedia)
sources.snippet: Exif data sits in APP1 as a TIFF-like structure; the GPS directory is reached through tag 0x8825, the Exif sub-directory through 0x8769, and the thumbnail is in the second directory.
sources.note: APP1 container, sub-directory pointer tags; agrees with the Exiv2 wiki on APP1

sources.title: NSRL test data (NIST)
sources.snippet: NIST's own page lists the SHA-256 digest of the ASCII string abc as BA7816BF 8F01CFEA 414140DE 5DAE2223 B00361A3 96177A9C B410FF61 F20015AD, for informal checking; it notes the examples date from FIPS 180-2.
sources.note: Primary-source SHA-256 example value (examples originate in the earlier FIPS 180-2)

sources.title: Test vectors for SHA-1, SHA-2 and SHA-3 (DI Management)
sources.snippet: Independent page listing SHA-2 test vectors, including the digest for abc and the longer 448-bit message.
sources.note: Independent agreement on the abc digest and source of further vectors

sources.title: FIPS 180-4: Secure Hash Standard (CSRC, NIST)
sources.snippet: NIST's official record of FIPS 180-4, which specifies SHA-1, SHA-224, SHA-256, SHA-384, SHA-512 and the truncated SHA-512 variants.
sources.note: Names the standard that defines SHA-256; page lists March 2012, other copies show 2015

sources.title: Why does Explorer show a thumbnail for my image that's different from the image? (The Old New Thing)
sources.snippet: A Microsoft engineer explains that a preview stored inside an image can be left stale by editing software, so a cropped photo may still show the pre-crop content, which is an information-disclosure risk.
sources.note: Documents the stale embedded thumbnail problem

sources.title: Editing JPEG photos, thumbnails and your privacy - edited out bits may still be visible
sources.snippet: Blog post warning that edited-out parts of a JPEG may remain visible in the embedded thumbnail.
sources.note: Independent second source for the thumbnail trap (title and result summary only)

sources.title: RedTeam Pentesting advisory RT-SA-2005-008
sources.snippet: Security advisory about image editors leaving the embedded thumbnail unchanged after cropping; a related CVE record treats it as a design flaw. The 20 percent and 2 percent figures in the result summary are not used.
sources.note: Third source on the thumbnail trap; statistics left out because the summary was blended

sources.title: Drupal issue 3583882 (image orientation after sanitising)
sources.snippet: A bug report where sanitising an image that had an orientation tag leaves it displayed in the wrong orientation; suggests rotating pixels first or keeping the tag.
sources.note: Orientation tag removal causes sideways display

sources.title: image orientation wrong (CocoConvert blog)
sources.snippet: Explains that software ignoring the orientation tag shows raw unrotated pixel data, so photos appear turned.
sources.note: Independent agreement on the orientation tag effect

sources.title: GPS Tags (ExifTool documentation)
sources.snippet: Lists the GPS tags stored in a separate directory in Exif, such as latitude as three rational numbers with a N or S reference letter, and the longitude and altitude equivalents.
sources.note: Field layout for the degrees-minutes-seconds worked example

sources.title: JPEGTRAN(1) manual page
sources.snippet: States that the tool cannot do lossy changes, yet while transforming image data losslessly it can drop metadata; a copy option controls what metadata is kept.
sources.note: Documents that metadata can be removed without re-encoding the picture

facts.claim: A JPEG file runs from a start marker (0xFFD8) to an end marker (0xFFD9); header segments start with a marker and a length, the scan header is followed directly by the compressed picture data, and Exif is stored in an APP1 segment (marker 0xFFE1) that contains a TIFF-style structure. Seen 2026-10-14.

In Exif, the GPS data is in its own sub-directory pointed to by tag 0x8825, the Exif sub-directory by tag 0x8769, and latitude is stored as three rational numbers plus an N or S reference letter. Seen 2026-10-14.

The SHA-256 digest of the ASCII text abc is ba7816bf 8f01cfea 414140de 5dae2223 b00361a3 96177a9c b410ff61 f20015ad, per NIST's NSRL test data page (examples carried over from FIPS 180-2) and an independent test-vector page. Seen 2026-10-14.
FIPS 180-4 is the NIST standard that specifies SHA-256 among the secure hash algorithms. Seen 2026-10-14 on NIST's CSRC page.

Editing software can leave the embedded Exif thumbnail unchanged after a crop, so the thumbnail may still show the original, uncropped scene (documented in a 2011 Microsoft engineer's blog post, a 2007 blog post and a 2005 security advisory).

Removing the Exif orientation tag without first rotating the pixels can leave a photo displayed sideways, because the stored pixels are unrotated and only the tag tells viewers to turn them. Seen 2026-10-14.
Metadata can be removed from a JPEG while the compressed picture data is passed through losslessly, according to the jpegtran manual page; no re-encoding of the picture is needed. Seen 2026-10-14.

design.coreLoop: Demo, question, aha: the visitor flips a switch on a parsed sample, sees the fields and the matching picture-data hash, answers a check question, then moves to the next rung (thumbnail trap, orientation catch, what stays). The optional drop-your-own step turns the same parser on their files, read-only unless they choose to download.
sophisticationHooks: A real, hand-written JPEG segment parser and writer in plain JavaScript that copies picture bytes untouched, with a lossless-ness check: the scan bytes before and after are compared byte by byte and by SHA-256
A from-scratch SHA-256 implementation verified in-page against NIST example vectors (abc, the empty message, the 448-bit message) with a visible pass badge
A TIFF directory walker handling both byte orders, pointer-following into the GPS, Exif and thumbnail directories, with bounds checks and a refusal path for malformed files
A decoded-field view with the degrees-minutes-seconds to decimal worked example, drawn on a plain coordinate grid with no map tiles or network
design.scopeForOneDay: Built: the segment-strip view, Exif field reader (GPS, camera, date, software), thumbnail and orientation demos on one bundled hand-made sample JPEG (a tiny picture with an invented place, an imaginary camera name and a fake date, base64-embedded), segment switches, SHA-256 proof panel with self-check, four check questions, intro and explainer text, and the More-toggled drop-your-own with cleaned downloads for JPEG only. Cut: formats other than JPEG, XMP/IPTC field decoding (shown as raw segments only), maker-note decoding, editing field values, map display, and any pixel re-encoding.
risks: Tag numbers 0x8825 and 0x8769 are seen only in search summaries of Wikipedia and ExifTool pages; the thumbnail tag numbers (0x0201, 0x0202) and compression value come from a page not recorded as a source, so the builder must check them against the Exif specification (CIPA DC-008) before coding.

Not confirmed by any opened page: no page was opened this run (WebFetch not attempted because the sandbox listed no working hosts); every source is search-only, so verified flags rest on two independent search results or on the standards body's own page.

NIST's page for the abc digest says its examples come from FIPS 180-2; the page will say 'NIST example value' and not claim they are printed in FIPS 180-4, and will list the other vectors as checked against the independent test-vector page.
The brief's claims that free web tools use batch caps or re-encode the picture were not checked; the page makes no claim about other tools or about paid products.

Maker notes are vendor-specific and may hold absolute offsets, so deleting or moving them is risky; the page deletes whole segments only and never rewrites inside the Exif block unless a rewrite path is built and tested, otherwise partial removal (GPS only) is shown as a rebuilt directory with a stated limit.

Partial removal (only GPS) requires rewriting the Exif block with fixed-up offsets; if that proves too risky in one morning, offer segment-level choices only (keep or drop all Exif, keep or drop comments) and keep the GPS-only view as a read-only highlight.
Canvas-made or user JPEGs vary: progressive files, multiple APP1 segments (XMP shares APP1), and files with trailing bytes must be handled by the parser or refused with a plain message.
Stripping the colour profile changes colour rendering and the orientation tag changes display; the page keeps both by default and explains why.
